title: Oracy and the Forgotten Third
author: Chris Wheadon
summary: Following Daisy Christodoulou's question about whether oracy might help the 'forgotten third' of pupils who struggle academically, Chris Wheadon presents data from two No More Marking oracy studies. The first involved 301 pupils from 57 schools and the second 107 matched pupils from 23 schools, aged 8 to 14, with spoken responses ranked by Comparative Judgement. Oracy correlated with written composition at 0.43, higher than the 0.34 in the published meta-analysis, so pupils weak at writing tend to be weak at speaking. Progress over a year was real but slowed with age, and the disadvantage gap of roughly 0.4 standard deviations resembled that in writing. Teachers asked what they rewarded named features such as sentence structure and the use of because, but and so. The conclusion is that oracy is not a hidden strength for struggling writers and that any oracy focus should target younger pupils, with the caveat that the samples are small.
points: Oracy and written composition correlated at 0.43 in the study, so pupils in the bottom third for writing are most likely also in the bottom third for oracy.
Oracy is not a hidden strength for pupils who struggle with writing, who tend to meet the same challenges in speech.
Improvement in oracy over a year slows with age, mirroring writing, which argues for focusing any effort on younger pupils.
The disadvantage gap in oracy was about 0.4 standard deviations, comparable to national English assessments.
Teachers judging speech independently rewarded sentence structure and conjunctions, features valued in writing.
quotes: Our advantage is that Comparative Judgement creates a fine grained measurement scale for oracy.

Our limitation, however, is that oracy is hard to assess, so unlike most of our other posts the samples in our study are small, which restricts the forms of analysis we can perform and limits our findings.
The correlation was 0.43, higher than the 0.34 reported in the meta-analysis1.
What is really striking is how improvement slows with age. Yes, these are small samples, but we see exactly the same in our writing composition data.

In both studies pupils with pupil premium status2 scored lower on average than the rest of the cohort. The gap is about 0.4 of a standard deviation3, broadly comparable with national English assessments at KS2.
Most of them mentioned features that are highly rated in written communication – including sentence structure.

Our findings suggest that oracy is not necessarily an area of hidden strength for pupils who struggle with writing: pupils encounter many of the same challenges in spoken and written expression, while teachers value similar features in each.
Finally, if we believe that oracy is a priority, then our data suggests it is the younger pupils we should focus on. Oracy, just like writing, gets harder to improve as pupils get older.
context: Comparative Judgement lets the studies measure oracy on a finer scale than the three national grades.
The authors admit small samples limit what the analysis can establish.
Oracy and writing correlate more strongly here than in the published meta-analysis.
Oracy progress slows with age just as writing progress does.
Disadvantaged pupils trail in oracy by a margin similar to writing.
Teachers reward written-style features such as sentence structure when judging speech.
Struggling writers are not hidden oracy stars, since both skills draw on shared challenges.
If oracy is prioritised, younger pupils offer the better return.
